Subject
Multimodal AI for Early Detection and Interpretation of Cardiac Disorders Using ECG and MRI Data
This internship focuses on the development of an intelligent medical decision-support system for the
detection, diagnosis, and prognosis of cardiac complications. The proposed framework aims to
integrate multimodal cardiac data, including electrocardiogram (ECG) signals, cardiac magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI/IRM), and associated clinical information, within advanced agentic AI
architectures. The internship will explore the integration of Large Language Models (LLMs),
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, knowledge graphs,
and domain-specific model fine tuning to build intelligent medical agents capable of supporting
clinicians throughout the cardiovascular diagnostic workflow.
ECG Signal Analysis

Section: 1. What is an ECG?
An ECG (electrocardiogram / électrocardiogramme) records the electrical activity of the heart over
time. Each heartbeat produces a repeating pattern of waves. The ECG captures and traces this
activity as a continuous curve.

Section: 1.1 How Are Signals Recorded?
Electrodes are placed on the skin (arms, legs, chest). Each pair of electrodes forms a lead that
captures the signal from a different angle.
• A standard ECG has 12 leads.
• 12 points of view on the same heart, at the same time.

Section: 1.2 Sampling Frequency
Sampling frequency is the number of measurements of the electrical signal taken per second.
• Higher frequency → more temporal detail.
• Higher frequency → heavier data (larger file size).

Section: 2. Data Science Perspective, Model Input
Each patient is represented as a matrix:
12 rows (leads) × 5,000 columns (time instants)
Each cell = a voltage in millivolts (mV) measured at a specific point in time.
Summary:
• 500 Hz = 500 points/second
• 10 seconds = 5,000 points per lead
• 12 leads → 60,000 values per patient
• Model input shape: (12, 5000) in mV
The model does not see an image. It receives a table of numbers: 12 columns (leads) × N rows
(time points). Each value is a voltage in millivolts.

Section: 3. How to Read an ECG
Every heartbeat follows a consistent sequence of electrical waves:
P → QRS → T
• In a healthy person, this cycle lasts about 0.6–1.0 seconds.
• The order and timing of these waves are identical across all 12 ECG leads.
• What changes from lead to lead is the appearance, shape, size, and direction.
• Each lead captures the same electrical event from a different angle.

Section: 3.1 The Waves
P Wave, small rounded bump
• Represents: Atrial نﯾذﻷا contraction (upper chambers push blood into ventricles).
• Normal duration: ~80–120 ms
• Abnormal if: Absent → atrial problem (e.g., atrial fibrillation)
QRS Complex, sharp spike (pointe)
• Represents: Ventricular contraction (ضﺎﺑﻘﻧا), the actual heartbeat. Most visible peak.
• Normal duration: ~80–100 ms
• Abnormal if: Wide and deformed → bundle branch block or ventricular arrhythmia
T Wave, wider bump
• Represents: Ventricular repolarization (ventricles recharge electrically).
• Abnormal if: Inverted or flattened → sign of ischemia (lack of oxygen to the heart)

Section: 3.2 The Intervals
RR Interval
• Definition: Distance between two consecutive R peaks
• Gives: Heart rate
• Abnormal if: Irregular → arrhythmia
PR Interval
• Definition: From the start of P to the start of QRS
• Measures: Atrial → ventricular conduction time
• Abnormal if: Too long → AV block
ST Segment
• Definition: The line between the end of QRS and the start of T
• Should be: On the baseline (isoelectric)
• Abnormal if: Elevated or depressed → possible myocardial infarction (heart attack)
QT Interval
• Definition: From the start of QRS to the end of T
• Abnormal if: Too long → risk of serious arrhythmia (e.g., Torsade de Pointes)

Section: 4. Feature Extraction, Three Levels of Analysis
When analyzing ECG data for machine learning, feature extraction can be conceptualized at three
complementary levels. Each corresponds to a different scale of observation.
Level Type of Comparison Domain Example
Level 1: Morphology Shape of a wave in a single lead Local QRS width
Level 2: Temporality Beat n vs beat n+1 (over time) Temporal RR interval
Level 3: Spatiality Lead X vs Lead Y (same instant) Spatial Electrical axis, R wave progression
Summary
• Level 1, Local (morphology): shape of a single wave.
• Level 2, Sequential (rhythm): organization of beats over time.
• Level 3, Multi-channel (spatiality): comparison across the 12 leads.

Section: 5.1 Atrial Fibrillation (AF)
A heart rhythm disorder where the atria (oreillettes) no longer contract in an organized way:
irregularity detection in beat sequences.
• ECG pattern: Absent P waves + irregularly irregular RR intervals
• Clinical note: Most common arrhythmia

Section: 5.2 ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
“STEMI-like myocardial infarction is the most serious type of heart attack, which is characterized by
a long interruption of blood supply. A troponin test measures the levels of troponin T or troponin I
proteins in the blood.” articles/MRI/2108.04016v2.pdf
A myocardial infarction (heart attack) with ST segment elevation.
• ECG pattern: ST elevation ≥1 mm in (dans au moins 2 leads adjacents) ≥2 contiguous leads +
reciprocal depression
Note:
- Elevation = the signal goes ABOVE the line
- Depression = the signal goes BELOW the line
when you see both in the same ECG at the same time, elevation in some leads, depression in
others, your model knows: this is a real MI, confirmed from two angles. That's the power of 12
leads working together.
The location of elevation and depression is not random at all. It follows a precise anatomical logic.
The heart has 4 walls. Each wall is "watched" by specific leads:
Wall Leads watching it Reciprocal leads (opposite)
Inferior (bottom) II, III, aVF I, aVL

Section: 5.3 Bundle Branch Blocks (LBBB / RBBB)
A bundle branch block is a delay or interruption in the electrical conduction through the ventricles.
Normalement, l’influx électrique part des oreillettes, passe par le nœud AV, puis se propage rapidement dans les
ventricules via deux “branches” (droite et gauche).
En résumé : c’est comme si un câble électrique était endommagé → le courant passe plus lentement ou par un détour, ce
qui déforme le signal.
• ECG pattern: Wide QRS >120 ms + specific lead patterns:
- RBBB (Right Bundle Branch Block) → typical RSR’ pattern in lead V1 (looks like two peaks).
- LBBB (Left Bundle Branch Block) → typical wide QS pattern in lead V1.
• Classification type: Morphology classification

Section: 5.4 Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH)
Increase in the muscle mass of the left ventricle.
Le ventricule gauche doit parfois travailler plus fort (par ex. en cas d’hypertension ou de valvule rétrécie).
Pour compenser, son muscle s’épaissit → il devient plus massif.
Résultat sur l’ECG : les ondes R sont beaucoup plus hautes (grande amplitude), car un muscle plus gros génère un
signal électrique plus fort.
En résumé : c’est comme si le “moteur” du ventricule gauche grossissait → il produit des signaux plus puissants, visibles
par des voltages élevés sur l’ECG.
• ECG pattern: High-voltage R waves
→ Simple rule: Sokolow- Lyon criterion : SV1+RV5
(S = amplitude of the S wave in V1, R = amplitude of the R wave in V5).
if the sum is ≥ 35 mm → LVH
→ Modified Cornell criterion: R wave in aVL > 1.2 mV → LVH
• Classification type: Voltage measurement task (un problème où on peut détecter/diagnostiquer la
pathologie juste en mesurant des valeurs de voltage sans avoir besoin d'analyser sa forme complexe, son
rythme, ou son évolution dans le temps → Juste une tâche de lecture d'amplitude à un point précis du signal
.)
MRI

Section: 1. What is an MRI?
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive medical imaging technique that uses strong
magnetic fields and radio waves to create detailed images of the organs and tissues inside the
body.

Section: 1.1 How Are MRIs Recorded?
Your body is mostly water. Water contains hydrogen atoms. MRI uses a strong magnet to align
those atoms, then fires radio waves to disturb them. As the atoms "snap back" to alignment, they
emit a signal. A computer turns that signal into an image.

Section: 1.2 Why MRI for the heart specifically ?
MRI is the gold standard for cardiac imaging because it can show things no other scan can :
- Heart movement : MRI films the heart beating in real time, you see how well the walls
contract
→ Function
- Scar (cicatriciel) tissue (fibrosis): Dead heart muscle from a past heart attack shows up as a
bright white patch, invisible on ECG
a “chamber” refers to one of the four cavities of the heart that fill with blood and pump it out.
→ Tissue damage
- Chamber (cavité cardiaque) size & wall thickness: Precise measurements of the ventricles,
is the heart enlarged? Is the wall too thick?
→ Structure
- Blood flow (irrigation)(perfusion): Contrast agent injected → shows which areas of the heart
muscle receive enough blood
→ Blood supply
Note: For our project: ECG shows the heart's electrical activity. MRI shows the heart's physical
state. Together they give a complete picture → that's exactly why multimodal AI is more powerful
than either alone.

Section: 4.1 Functional abnormalities (from Cine MRI)
This is about how well the heart moves, not what it looks like structurally. Cine MRI is a video, so
it's the natural sequence to catch motion problems.
● Heart failure (reduced EF): The ventricle isn't pumping out enough blood per beat. Split
into two types clinically — HFrEF (reduced ejection fraction, the "classic" weak-pump failure)
and HFpEF (preserved EF, where the muscle still pumps a normal %, but the heart doesn't
fill properly — stiffer walls). Cine MRI alone gives you EF, so HFrEF is directly detectable;
HFpEF needs the volumes/filling pattern too.
● Wall motion abnormalities: Instead of looking at the whole heart's EF, you look segment by
segment (the heart is usually divided into 16–17 standard segments). A segment can be
hypokinetic (moving weakly), akinetic (not moving at all), or dyskinetic (moving the wrong
way — bulging outward when it should contract). This is usually a sign of localized damage,
e.g. from a blocked artery feeding that specific segment.
● Dyssynchrony: Normally all walls contract together, in sync. If one wall contracts late
relative to the others, the pump becomes mechanically inefficient even if overall EF looks
okay-ish.

Section: 4.2 Structural abnormalities (from Cine MRI + short axis stack)
This is about the heart's shape and size, which you get by combining the moving Cine images
with the full 3D stack (base-to-apex slices).
● Dilated (dilatée) cardiomyopathy (DCM): The ventricle chamber is enlarged/stretched out,
and the walls are thin. Think of it like a balloon that's been overstretched: it holds more
volume but pumps less effectively. Usually goes along with low EF (Elle s’accompagne
généralement d’une fraction d’éjection basse).
● Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM): The opposite shape problem: walls are abnormally
thick, chamber can be normal or small. Often genetic. Dangerous because thick muscle can
obstruct blood flow and is linked to sudden cardiac events, especially in young athletes.

Section: 4.3 Tissue/scar abnormalities (from LGE)
This is about permanent damage, using the contrast agent that lights up dead tissue.
● Prior myocardial infarction: A past heart attack leaves a scar. LGE shows two patterns
that matter clinically: subendocardial (scar only in the inner layer, typical of a "classic"
ischemic infarct) vs transmural (scar through the full wall thickness, meaning more severe
damage, worse prognosis). The pattern location also usually matches which coronary artery
was blocked.
● Sudden death risk (via LGE extent %): This isn't a separate disease, it's a quantitative risk
score: the more scar tissue (as % of total heart muscle), the higher risk of dangerous
arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. This is a good regression target alongside EF for
your project, since it's continuous, not just a yes/no label.

Section: 4.4 Inflammatory / infiltrative disease (from T1/T2 mapping)
This is about tissue composition: problems that don't show up as motion issues or old scars (ne
se manifestent pas par des troubles de la mobilité ou de vieilles cicatrices), but as changes at the
tissue level (inflammation, deposits, swelling) (par des changements au niveau des tissus
(inflammation, dépôts, gonflement)).
● Myocarditis (acute inflammation):Shows up as elevated T2 (edema/inflammation) and
sometimes elevated T1.
● Edema: Swelling from excess fluid in the tissue (accumulation excessive de liquide dans les
tissus): can be a marker of acute injury (lésion aiguë (ةدﺎﺣ ﺔﻓآ)) (e.g., very recent heart attack,
before scar has even formed) or inflammation. Elevated T2 is the key signal.
● Œdème : gonflement dû à une accumulation excessive de liquide dans les tissus – peut être
un marqueur de (par exemple, un infarctus du myocarde très récent, avant même la
formation d’une cicatrice) ou d’inflammation. Une élévation du T2 est le signal clé.

The biggest difference for our model
ECG is a lightweight 1D signal, easy to load, fast to train on. MRI is a heavy 3D or 4D volume,
memory-intensive, requires GPU, needs careful preprocessing. This is why most papers process
them with separate encoders and fuse later.
Analogy : ECG is an audio file. MRI is a movie. You wouldn't process audio and video with the same
architecture, same logic applies here.
→ In our project architecture: ECG encoder (1D-CNN / Transformer) + MRI encoder (2D or 3D
CNN) → fusion layer → LLM reasoning → diagnosis output.

We follow the preprocessing pipeline of [1], with the addition of R-peak detection using the
Pan-Tompkins algorithm for rhythm feature extraction.
Our ECG preprocessing pipeline consists of the following steps:
Baseline Wander Removal:
Baseline wander is a low frequency artifact in ECG signals caused by patient movement,
respiration, or poor electrode contact.
This artifact is a very low-frequency component (< 0.5 Hz) overlapping (se superposent au signal utile)
the useful ECG signal.
We implemented a high-pass filter with a cutoff (filtre passe-haut) frequency of 0.5 Hz to remove
baseline wander while preserving the morphological characteristics (P, QRS, and T waves) of the
ECG signal.
→ Isolate low-frequency artifacts from the physiological signal of interest (contenu physiologique
pertinent).
Powerline Interference Removal:

Section: 4.4 Inflammatory / infiltrative disease (from T1/T2 mapping)
Powerline interference (Les lignes électriques = le courant alternatif (AC) qui alimente nos maisons, hôpitaux,
ordinateurs, etc) manifests as 50 Hz (Europe, Africa, Asia) or 60 Hz (North America) noise (les
électrodes ECG, très sensibles, peuvent capter ce champ électromagnétique → cela crée un bruit sinusoïdal superposé
au signal cardiaque: on observe un bourdonnement régulier superposé au tracé ECG, qui masque les petites ondes (P, T)
et déforme la lecture) in ECG signals due to electromagnetic interference from power lines.
We applied a notch filter (filtre coupe-bande) centered at 50/60 Hz (depending on the geographical
region of data collection) with a narrow bandwidth of 2 Hz to remove this interference without
affecting adjacent frequency components(supprime uniquement cette fréquence parasite sans toucher aux
autres composantes utiles du signal ECG).
Wavelet Denoising:
ECG signals often contain high-frequency noise (muscle activity, sensors, environment). This
noise can obscure sharp features (masquer les détails fins) like QRS complexes.
To remove high-frequency noise while preserving the sharp features of ECG signals (such as QRS

Section: 4.4 Inflammatory / infiltrative disease (from T1/T2 mapping)
complexes), we employed wavelet denoising.
Wavelet transform decomposes the signal into multiple scales (frequency bands). (Les ondelettes
permettent de décomposer le signal en plusieurs échelles (fréquences). On peut ainsi isoler le bruit (présent dans les
hautes fréquences) et préserver les composantes physiologiques)
● Low-frequency components (approximations) retain the global morphology of the ECG
(P and T waves).
● High-frequency components (details) capture rapid oscillations, where noise is
concentrated.
Specifically, we used a 5-level decomposition with the Daube chies 6 (db6) wavelet, which has been
shown to capture ECG morphology effectively. We apply soft thresholding ( seuil doux ) to the detail
coefficients using a threshold determined by the universal threshold method (√(2log(N)) × σ, where
N is the signal length and σ is the noise standard deviation estimated from the first-level detail
coefficients).
By reducing high-frequency detail coefficients and reconstructing the signal, wavelet denoising
effectively removes noise while maintaining the integrity of ECG morphology.
Daubechies 6 (db6) = a specific wavelet function used in decomposition.

Section: 4.4 Inflammatory / infiltrative disease (from T1/T2 mapping)
Chosen for ECG because it matches the morphology of ECG signals (sharp + smooth parts).
Role in denoising: separates noise (high-frequency details) from useful signal (approximations).
Signal Normalization:
ECG signals often vary in amplitude due to patient differences, electrode placement, or recording
devices.
Inconsistent scales make it difficult to compare signals and can bias machine learning models.
We apply statistical normalization → adjust the signal to have zero mean and unit variance to
ensure consistent amplitude ranges across different recordings and to facilitate model training.

R-Peak Detection in ECG Preprocessing
To analyze heart rhythm, we need to identify beats.
● The R-peak is the maximum point of the QRS complex, which represents ventricular
depolarization (dépolarisation ventriculaire: le moment où les ventricules (les deux chambres inférieures du
cœur) s'activent électriquement pour se contracter et éjecter le sang. ) (the main pumping action of the heart),
used for: heart rate, HRV, arrhythmia detection. The R-peak is its maximum and serves as

Section: 4.4 Inflammatory / infiltrative disease (from T1/T2 mapping)
a temporal marker.
We apply a detection algorithm, most commonly the Pan-Tompkins algorithm.
○ Steps: filtering → differentiation (dérivation) → squaring → moving window integration → adaptive
thresholding.
○ Each detected R-peak allows computation of RR intervals (time between consecutive beats).
→ converts a continuous ECG signal into discrete events (heartbeats), enabling heart rate and
rhythm variability analysis.

Electrocardiography (ECG) is a key non-invasive diagnostic tool for cardiovascular diseases which is
increasingly supported by algorithms based on machine learning. Major obstacles for the development
of automatic ECG interpretation algorithms are both the lack of public datasets and well-defined
benchmarking procedures to allow comparison s of different algorithms. To address these issues, we put
forward PTB-XL, the to-date largest freely accessible clinical 12-lead ECG-waveform dataset comprising
21837 records from 18885 patients of 10 seconds length. The ECG-waveform data was annotated by
up to two cardiologists as a multi-label dataset, where diagnostic labels were further aggregated into
super and subclasses. the dataset covers a broad range of diagnostic classes including, in particular,
a large fraction of healthy records. the combination with additional metadata on demographics,

additional diagnostic statements, diagnosis likelihoods, manually annotated signal properties as
well as suggested folds for splitting training and test sets turns the dataset into a rich resource for the
development and the evaluation of automatic ECG interpretation algorithms.
Background & Summary
Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of mortality worldwide, which is in high-income countries only
surpassed by cancer1. Electrocardiography (ECG) provides a key non-invasive diagnostic tool for assessing
the cardiac clinical status of a patient. Advanced decision support systems based on automatic ECG interpre-
tation algorithms promise significant assistance for the medical personnel due to the large number of ECGs
that are routinely taken. However, there are at least two major obstacles that restrict the progress in this field
beyond the demonstration of exceptional performance of closed-source algorithms on custom datasets with
restricted access2,3, (1) the lack of large publicly available datasets for training and validation4, and (2) the lack
of well-defined evaluation procedures for these algorithms. We aim to address both issues and to close this gap

Section: (document start)
in the research landscape by putting forward PTB-XL5, a clinical ECG dataset of unprecedented size along with
proposed folds for the evaluation of machine learning algorithms.
The raw signal data underlying the PTB-XL dataset was recorded by devices from the Schiller AG between
October 1989 and June 1996. The transfer of the raw data into a structured database, its curation along with the
development of corresponding ECG analysis algorithms was a long term project at the Physikalisch Technische
Bundesanstalt (PTB). These efforts resulted in a number of publications6–11, but the access to the dataset remained
restricted until now. The dataset comprises 21837 clinical 12-lead ECG records of 10 seconds length from 18885
patients. The dataset is balanced with respect to sex (52% male and 48% female) and covers the whole range of
ages from 0 to 95 years (median 62 and interquantile range of 22). The ECG records were annotated by up to two
cardiologists with potentially multiple ECG statements out of a set of 71 different statements conforming to the
SCP-ECG standard12. The statements cover form, rhythm and diagnostic statements in a unified,

Section: (document start)
machine-readable form. For the diagnostic labels we provide a hierarchical organization in terms of 5 coarse
superclasses and 24 subclasses for the diagnostic labels, see Fig. 1 for a graphical summary of the dataset, that
allow for different levels of granularity. Besides annotations in the form of ECG statements along with likelihood
information for diagnostic statements, additional metadata for example in the form of manually annotated signal
quality statements are available.
Apart from the outstanding nominal size of PTB-XL, the dataset is distinguished by its diversity, both in terms
of signal quality (with 77.01% of highest signal quality) but also in terms of a rich coverage of pathologies, many

Cross-validation Folds. For comparability of machine learning algorithms trained on PTB-XL, we provide fold
assignments (strat_fold) for all ECG records that can be used to implement recommended train-test splits.
The incentive to use stratified sampling is to reduce bias and variance of score estimations, see17. In addition,
it leads to a test set distribution for holdout evaluation that mimics the training set distribution as closely as
possible to disentangle aspects of covariate shift/dataset shift from the evaluation procedure. We extend existing
multilabel stratification methods from the literature to achieve a balanced label while additionally providing two
distinguished folds with a particularly high label quality. During this process, each record is assigned to one of
ten folds, where the tenth fold is intended to be used for holdout set evaluation and the penultimate ninth fold is
supposed to be used as validation set, see Prediction Tasks and Train-Test-Splits for ML Algorithms in Usage Notes
for a more detailed description. The fold assignment always respects the underlying patient assignments. This

The proposed procedure extends existing stratified sampling methods from the literature18 by accounting for
sampling based on patients and by optionally incorporating quality constraints for certain folds. To achieve not
only a balanced label distribution but also a balanced age and sex distribution, we do not only incorporate all ECG
statements but also sex and age (in five bins each covering 20 years). All ECG statements, sex and age for a given
patient are appended into a single list with potentially non-unique entries to ensure sampling based on patients.
Then the labels are distributed label-by-label as proposed18, starting with the least populated label within the
remaining records. Patients with ECG records that are annotated with this label are subsequently distributed onto

the folds. If there is a unique fold that is in most need of the given label, all ECGs of the patient that is currently
under consideration are assigned to this fold. In case of a tie, the assignment proceeds by trying to balance the
overall sizes of the candidate folds.
During this process, we keep track of the quality of the ECG annotations. A patient is considered clean if for
all corresponding ECGs validated_by_human is set to true. When assigning ECGs from a patient that does
not carry this flag, we exclude the ninth and tenth fold from the set of folds the samples can be assigned to. As
the dataset and in particular the ratio of clean vs. non-clean patients is large enough, the sampling procedure still
leads to a label distribution in the clean folds that still approximates the overall distribution of labels and sexes in
the dataset very well, see Fig. 6.
We believe that this procedure is of general interest for multi-label datasets with multiple records per patient
and, in particular in the current context, for exploring the impact of different stratification methods. For the fold

Quality assessment for Waveform Data. Since we present the waveform data in its original (binary)
form without any modifications (apart from saving it in WFDB-format), we expect a lot of variability with respect

the signal data by an technical expert briefly. The signal quality was quantified by a person with technical exper-
tise according to the following categories:
• baseline_drift for global drifts in 7.36% of the signal.
• static_noise for noisy signals and burst_noise for noise peaks, set for 14.94% and 2.81% of records
retrospectively.
• electrodes_problems for individual problems with electrodes (0.14% of records).

resource for the training and the evaluation of ECG analysis algorithms. Whereas a comprehensive discussion
of possible prediction tasks that can be investigated based on the dataset is clearly beyond the format of this data

tasks that try to infer different subsets of ECG statements from the ECG record. These tasks can typically be
framed as multi-label classification problems. Although a thorough description of proposed evaluation metrics
would go beyond of the scope of this manuscript, we highly recommend macro-averaged and threshold-free
metrics, such as the macro-averaged area under the receiver operating curve (AUROC). Micro-averaged metrics
would overrepresent highly populated classes, whose distribution just reflects the data collection process rather
than the statistical distribution of the different pathologies in the population. The large number of more than 2000
patients with multiple ECGs potentially allows to develop prediction models for future cardiac conditions or their
progression from previously collected ECGs. Beyond ECG statement prediction, the dataset allows for age/sex
inference from the raw ECG record and to develop ECG quality assessment algorithms based on the signal qual-

For comparability of machine learning algorithms trained on PTB-XL, we provide recommended train-test
splits in the form of assignments of the record to one of ten cross-validation folds. We propose to use the tenth
fold, which is ensured to contain only ECGs that have certainly be validated by at least one human cardiologist
and are therefore presumably of highest label quality, to separate a test set that is only used for the final perfor-
mance evaluation of a proposed algorithm. The remaining nine folds can be used as training and validation set
and split at one’s own discretion potentially utilizing the recommended fold assignments. As the ninth and the
tenth fold satisfy the same quality criteria, we recommend to use the ninth fold as validation set.

Abstract
Cardiovascular diseases remain a leading cause of mortality worldwide, necessitating accurate and timely diagnosis.
Electrocardiogram (ECG) and phonocardiogram (PCG) signals provide complementary information about cardiac
function, electrical and mechanical activity, respectively. In this study, we propose a multimodal deep learning
framework that integrates ECG and PCG using a dual-branch CNN–BiLSTM–SE architecture with cross-modal atten-
tion. Our preprocessing pipeline includes wavelet denoising, adaptive filtering, and normalization, with parameters
tuned for each dataset’s noise profile. We evaluate the model on multiple datasets: MIT-BIH Arrhythmia (47 subjects),
PTB Diagnostic ECG (290 subjects), PhysioNet PCG Challenge 2016 (3126 subjects), PhysioNet PCG Challenge 2022

data augmentation techniques:

account for variations in signal alignment.
• Amplitude Scaling: Random scaling of signal ampli-
tude by a factor between 0.8 and 1.2 to account for
variations in signal strength.
• Gaussian Noise Addition: Addition of Gaussian noise
with a signal-to-noise ratio between 15 and 25 dB to
simulate recording noise.
• Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique
(SMOTE): Generation of synthetic samples for
underrepresented classes based on their feature
